title: How feasible is vibe-coding a physics-based sports game?
author: SnooRegrets9506
selftext:
Preface this by saying, I have essentially no coding skill or experience, but my general question is: is it feasible at all with the state of current models to vibe-code a prototype of a physics-based, multiplayer sports game? 

And then to follow up--and I know this is a very open-ended question-- if it IS feasible, is it something someone like me should even bother trying? 

Seems like a lot here are making RPG/Adventure or FPS games, so I was wondering how much more (or less) would be involved with what I’m thinking. The idea is essentially Rocket League-esque, but ice hockey. Player models gliding around on ice, bumping into each other and slapping a puck around a fully physics-based environment. Very simple in concept, but I would anticipate that the complexity in designing it would be to get the gameplay feel and physical interactions dialed in just right so as to make it very tactile and intuitive, while allowing for a high skill ceiling.

I have no pie-in-the-sky ambitions, it’s just something that as a long-time sports gamer and hobbyist game designer (card and board games, not digital), I have always wanted to see, and I’m wondering if the time is ripe with AI to give it a go. Give me your honest thoughts, and in fact I’d love to hear, “yeah, don’t waste your time and money” from folks knowledgeable about it. I would be approaching it as a fun, long-term hobby, and I do have some friends with tech skill that I would try to get involved if I was actually able to make something functional, but I don’t want to go down a ridiculously daunting technical road.

comments.author: arcarsenal986
comments.body: A lot of games do low friction surfaces already, the best way to find out is to just try it.

comments.author: FancyName_132
comments.body:
Yes it's possible.  
Only you can know if it's worth it, do you want to make a game for yourself ? publish it ? Sell it ? Just for the fun or making it ? You can get pretty far on a $20/mo subscription with Opus 5.5 so give it a try, see if you like the process

comments.author: Nostradamivre
comments.body:
“Yeah, don’t waste your time and money”: man, if it makes you happy, trying new things and exploring is NOT a waste of time or money! I’m making a horror game for my wife. It will never reach Steam or anything, but that’s not the goal.

As for your project, I think a sports/physics-based game is actually not that hard. There’s plenty of source material, videos, and written explanations out there to use as reference, so I’d definitely give it a try!

comments.author: SylvanCreatures
comments.body: A lot depends on your expectations, and your approach. You could get a prototype going in a day, but then building that prototype into something shippable will take considerably more time. There are a million weird little things to actually shipping, from if you use a particular engine (Unreal, Unity, Godot, etc) or write it from scratch, want it on PC or Mobile or Console, how and what you want your art to be, and most importantly, tuning the game loop to be fun! So it is possible, but it isn’t just a day, unless all you want is a “look what I vibe coded” demo.

replies.author: SnooRegrets9506
replies.body: Oh not a one-shot thing at all, I’d be planning on working on it bit by bit over months or years, with no real goal other than seeing if I can come close to my vision. Thanks for the response!

replies.author: SylvanCreatures
replies.body: That’s probably the best approach, honestly. I’d keep it simple, stay in greybox and gameplay tuning as long as you can, and hit the visual presentation as late as possible. You have no investors to please, so you can spend the dev time on the gameplay, not expensive visual explorations. Personally, I would skip the “game engines” and do it all from scratch, it will save you the trouble of adapting someone else’s generic frameworks into your highly specific vision. Your mileage may vary of course.

replies.author: SnooRegrets9506
replies.body: You mean instead of developing it within Unity, etc., code the engine from scratch? THAT sounds daunting…when I say I have essentially no coding skills, I mean it, lol.

replies.author: SylvanCreatures
replies.body: So using an engine off the shelf gives you a lot of generic capability, and the trap is spending your dev time “learning the engine” instead of working on your game. Presuming you are a team of 1, building from scratch (or just using things like OpenGL, Metal, Vulkan, etc) lets your game logic  and abstractions be purpose driven, rather than bending someone else’s architecture into the shape of your game. Also, engines often come with strings attached. On the flip side having a community of other devs using the same tech is nice, shared burdens and all that.

replies.author: SnooRegrets9506
replies.body: Appreciate the insight, that’s interesting. Big studios will typically develop within an engine though, no? Rocket League, for instance I believe runs in Unreal…why wouldn’t a studio like that want the more granular control of their physics like you describe?

replies.author: SylvanCreatures
replies.body: Many studios use custom engines, others choose off the shelf. Trade offs include things like hiring people who know the engine, vs having to train people on a new system, total control vs engine features, and of course what strings you are willing to put up with. Many studios have migrated to Unreal because of the ease of finding employees and outsourcing studios that can “drop in” to the workflow. Most mobile devs choose Unity for ease of cross platform development.

comments.author: Trojanheadcoach
comments.body: Very possible to make the physics and a core gameplay you think is fun. Impossible to get big studio quality on the player models and animations

comments.author: Nomski88
comments.body: I programmed a fully functional 3D engine using local AI :) and I'm not talking three.js

comments.author: InternetMagic_n_Tech
comments.body:
Probably not easy ... Possible... I don't think so

Whatever you do get it to write unit tests. That way you at least know something breaks

replies.author: SylvanCreatures
replies.body: Setting up rules up front, especially unit tests saves so much time!

replies.author: InternetMagic_n_Tech
replies.body: Well the unit tests will need updates over time but it's better than just yeeting your tokens to the wind because of a bad prompt

comments.author: Hungry-Fig-8640
comments.body:
Im actually doing something similar, arcade sports games are a niche genre that can be good if done right, but i haven't seen a game of the genre that stood out for a minute. Take what you like about hockey, add in some wacky mechanic and playtest till it's fun and if it isn't change something and start again. 

Look into the level of determinism for the physics in whatever game engine you go for and if its non-existent, code your own physics for the puck, with a bit of research you can do it. That's the main character of your game, get the feel of hitting that you want and then work on multiplayer and replication, add mechanics or features one by one and see how it feels as a whole before continuing. Iterate.

You will have to put in effort at some point and be willing to "waste money and time" if you ever want to do something meaningful.

replies.author: SnooRegrets9506
replies.body:
Cool, that’s exactly how I would plan to approach it. 

And yeah, I’m not looking to one-shot anything or cut corners, I just wanted to see how many might say, “that is a tough thing to develop if you don’t know what you’re doing , even with AI,” and weigh that in my decisions.

comments.author: jugger_naughtyy
comments.body: Its possible but requires hundreds of hours of twisting knobs and level design. It would still take a year or two.

comments.author: spoffenbaugh
comments.body:
I think that physics based games with instant feedback on if it feels fun or not is a great place to start. The hardest part is animations. I did a racing game first because animations are very limited there.

You should check out a game called Center Ice Hockey on steam. I am not sure, but it feels like it used AI. The intertia on the ice feels very good on that one
